props.title: Crash and Burn

sections.content: **Crash and Burn** (1990) emerges from the post-apocalyptic B-movie boom of the late 1980s and early 1990s, following the success of **Mad Max** (1979) and its sequels. Produced by Charles Band's Full Moon Entertainment, it fits into that peculiar niche of low-budget sci-fi that dominated direct-to-video shelves. Despite its modest budget, the film attempts ambitious cyberpunk themes similar to **RoboCop** (1987) and **Hardware** (1990), featuring a dystopian 2030 where synthetic humans and corporate control create a tense atmosphere.

sections.content: The early 1990s saw a fascinating convergence of cyberpunk themes and post-apocalyptic settings in lower-budget films. **Circuitry Man** (1990) and **Cyborg** (1989) exemplified this trend, mixing chrome and grime in stories about technological downfall. These films often featured practical effects and stop-motion animation, giving them a tactile quality missing from later CGI-heavy productions.

Full Moon Entertainment specialized in ambitious genre films on tight budgets, creating a distinctive visual style that influenced direct-to-video sci-fi. Their other releases like **Robot Wars** (1993) and **Arcade** (1993) continued exploring similar themes of artificial intelligence and corporate dystopia, often achieving impressive results through creative practical effects and model work. sections.content: The direct-to-video market of the late 1980s and early 1990s provided fertile ground for experimental sci-fi storytelling. While major studios focused on bigger budgets, companies like Full Moon and Empire Pictures filled the gap with films like **Trancers** (1984) and **Zone Troopers** (1985). These smaller productions often took more risks with their narratives, mixing genres and pushing boundaries in ways mainstream films couldn't.
